svg.text: PowerMonger: one simulation tick and the entity iterator
The tick body $13000 runs every call; only the present-rate block sits behind the $57ff0/$57fee divider
PowerMonger (Bullfrog / Electronic Arts, 1990) is a war game on a height-mapped land of settlements: the player gives orders to captains,
the computer lords give orders through the same path, and every man carries them out on his own. The game advances in ticks. Each tick
runs the routine $13000 once, and that routine moves the whole world one step: the commander AI decides, every man, boat and building
takes one step of its own small state machine, and the screen is redrawn.
The figure shows one tick. Left: the calls $13000 makes, in order. Right: the loop $14b62 that walks every object record once and jumps to
the handler for its current mode. Lower right: the other data pools the same tick moves. The point to take away is that there is no
separate AI per unit type (observed in every record traced, not proven absent): a record holds a mode number, the loop runs that mode's
handler, and the handler's choice of the next mode is the behaviour.

g.text: side pools: animals, pigeons, arrows, forest
order executor: $58016 -> group state, lead mode
The iterator $14b62: one pass per tick
D6, D7 := x, y (bytes 8, 10); D0 := mode, byte 31
one tick of the mode handler ($14c48..$1620e, ai.md)
epilogue: $161c4 clamp + terrain veto (water: mode $00) + relink;
What shares the tick: the pools
The bucket chains link all pools by offsets from $51b66 (negative below it).

svg.text: How to read each panel
The tick (left)
Each row is one call made by $13000, top to bottom
in the order it runs: the routine's address, what
it does, and a fill for how sure we are (legend at
the foot). The two purple italic lines are not
calls; they mark where the drawing block behind
the divider starts and ends.
Takeaway: the commander AI $6522, the entity loop
$14b62 and the order executor $6a3a run on every
tick. Only the four drawing calls $1870, $12ce0,
$178ae and $f898 sit behind the divider, and at
normal speed the divider is 1, so they run every
tick too.
The iterator (right)
A flowchart for one record; the arrow on the right
goes back for the next record until the end of the
array. Byte 5 is the owner: 0 is a free slot,
negative a dying man, positive a live one. A live
record's mode (byte 31) indexes a table of 75
handler offsets at $14bb4.
Takeaway: one jump table replaces any per-type
logic. The handler moves the record one tick and
usually writes a new mode; the epilogue clamps the
position, vetoes a step onto water by setting mode
$00, and relinks the record into its map-cell
bucket.
The pools (lower right)
One row per data pool: what it holds, its base
address and record size, and the routine that
moves it each tick. "511 x 50 B" means 511 records
of 50 bytes.
Takeaway: only men, boats, buildings and markers
are object records. Animals, pigeons, arrows and
trees are smaller pools moved near the top of the
tick. The cell buckets let a man find neighbours
by walking one chain instead of scanning all 511
records.
Numbers and how we know them
Cadence, from a 3-million-instruction trace of mission 1: 13 ticks per 250 VBLs (the ST's screen interrupt, one per displayed frame), about 2.6 ticks
a second; one tick costs about 19 VBLs of instructions, so the game is limited by computation, not by the display. $6522, $d322, $3e06 and $6a3a ran
13 times each in that trace, $14b62 14 times. One tick is about 200k to 230k emulated instructions ("steps").
A man, boat, building or marker is one 50-byte record and runs its mode handler once per tick inside $14b62. Animals, pigeons, arrows and trees are
separate pools moved by $3e06 near the top of the same tick; they are not entity records. Mission 1, settled view: about 50 of the 511 slots are in
use and about 26 reach a handler each tick.
Proven means a gate passed: a Python rewrite of the routine was run beside the game's own 68000 code, called in isolation from many saved states (the
emulator's callcap command), and every changed byte matched; "675/675" is matching bytes out of bytes compared. Proven here: the $14b62 prologue and
epilogues (675/675 and 1335/1335 tracked bytes), the dying path $1623c 275/275, animals and pigeons 45094/45094, arrows 4210/4210, the forest animator
$4342 8 of 9 branches. Live: the trace counts above. Code read: the call-order listing, read from the disassembly. A $ value is a RAM address in the
game, cited so it can be checked.
Evidence:
proven (gate vs the real 68000)
live (seen running, counted)
code read
